title: Read the room first: function, balance and colour

say: Read the room first: function, balance and colour.
This is the video for module one of Interior Decoration Basics: how decorators see a room.
Professionals start with three questions. First, what is this room for? Sleeping, receiving guests, studying, or selling to customers?

say: Before you move a single chair, photograph the room from every corner and the doorway. Then check five things. Light: where do the windows face, and which bulbs are fitted?

panel.heading: The five-point check
items: Light: windows, bulbs, dark corners
Flow: can people walk through easily?
Clutter and storage
Colour and condition
Climate: heat, dust, power cuts, cleaning

say: Flow: can people walk from the door to the seats without squeezing past furniture?

say: Every object has visual weight. Large, dark or bright things look heavier. A room feels balanced when that weight is spread so no side seems to tip over. Symmetrical balance is a mirror image on both sides. It feels formal and calm.

panel.heading: Two ways to balance a room
right: One sofa, balanced by two chairs

say: Asymmetrical balance uses different items of equal weight, like one sofa balanced by two chairs. Halima's client had all the heavy furniture on one wall. Moving the tall cabinet to the opposite wall balanced the room without buying anything.

panel.heading: Two ways to balance a room
right: One sofa, balanced by two chairs

say: A centre table is often about two-thirds the length of the sofa, so people can reach it from each seat.

panel.heading: Rules of thumb that work
items: Centre table about two-thirds of sofa length
One clear focal point; seats face it
Repeat each accent colour three times
Rug under at least the front legs
Picture centres about 1.5 m from the floor

say: Give the room one focal point, like a feature wall, a framed adire panel, or a neatly styled TV wall. Arrange seats to face it, and keep other walls quieter.

say: Divide a room's colour roughly into 60% dominant colour, usually the walls. Bisi's client loved an indigo adire fabric with rust-orange details, so Bisi chose soft, warm off-white walls.

panel.heading: The 60-30-10 rule
items: 60%: dominant colour, walls
30%: secondary, sofa, curtains, rug
10%: accent, cushions, vases, art
Test paint patches morning, afternoon, night

say: 30% secondary colour: indigo adire curtains and a mid-blue bedspread.

say: 10% accent: rust-orange cushions, a clay pot and a picture frame, repeating the accent three times.

say: Light changes colour, so paint a patch about the size of an A3 sheet and look at it in the morning, afternoon and at night before the client chooses.

panel.rule: Screens lie. Confirm colours with real samples in the real room.

say: You are learning decoration, not structural work. Moving sockets, adding ceiling lights, removing walls or changing plumbing must be done by qualified people. You can coordinate them, but say in writing that their work is their responsibility.

cards.d: Moving sockets, ceiling lights, walls or plumbing must be done by qualified people.
Keep windows and doors open while painting and until the smell fades.
Keep paint and thinners away from children and flames. Read the tin.

say: Keep windows and doors open while painting and until the smell fades, and take breaks in fresh air.

say: To remember. Start with function, users and problems. Take before photos from every corner. Spread the visual weight and give the room one focal point. Use 60-30-10. And test real paint in morning, afternoon and night light.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Function, users, problems come first
Before photos from every corner
Spread visual weight; one focal point
60% dominant, 30% secondary, 10% accent
Test real paint in three lights
